summary: This partial document is the cover and table of contents of JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s Form 10‑Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2021 (Commission file no. 1‑5805). It provides registrant details (Delaware incorporation, EIN 13‑2624428, 383 Madison Avenue, New York, NY), contact information, and securities listings, including common stock (JPM) on the NYSE, multiple preferred stock depositary share series, an Alerian MLP Index ETN (AMJ) on NYSE Arca, and a guarantee of callable notes (JPM/28) on the NYSE. title: INTRODUCTION
heading: INTRODUCTION
start_phrase: The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for the first quarter of 2021 .
summary:
- Introduces JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s MD&A for the first quarter of 2021, to be read alongside the 2020 Form 10-K and supported by a glossary and LOB metrics.
- Notes inclusion of forward-looking statements subject to significant risks and uncertainties, with cross-references to related disclosures in this Form 10-Q and the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Provides a firm overview: a Delaware-incorporated (1968) U.S.-based global financial services leader with $3.7 trillion in assets and $280.7 billion in stockholders’ equity as of March 31, 2021, serving consumers, small businesses, and major corporate, institutional, and government clients under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands.
- Describes organizational structure and key entities: principal bank subsidiary JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (branches in 38 states and D.C.); principal non-bank subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; and principal non-U.S. operating subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.).
- Outlines management reporting segments: four major reportable businesses—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment, with references to notes for detailed segment descriptions.
- Highlights investor communications and access: SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) made available free on the firm’s website shortly after filing, with additional information via the Investor Relations site.
text:
INTRODUCTION
The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the 
financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of 
JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for 
the first  quarter of 2021 . 
This Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the first  quarter of 
2021  (“Form 10-Q”) should be read together with JPMorgan 
Chase’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended 
December 31, 2020  (“2020  Form 10-K”). Refer to the 
Glossary of terms and acronyms and line of business (“LOB”) 
metrics on pages 163-171  for definitions of terms and 
acronyms used throughout this Form 10-Q.
The MD&A c ontains forward-looking statements within the 
meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 
1995. These forward-looking statements are based on the 
current beliefs and expectations of JPMorgan Chase’s 
management, speak only as of the date of this Form 10-Q and 
are subject to significant risks and uncertainties. Refer to 
Forward-looking Statements on page 78  of this Form 10-Q, 
Part II, Item 1A, Risk Factors on pages 172-173  of this Form 
10-Q and Part I, Item 1A, Risk factors, on pages 8-32 of the 
2020  Form 10-K for a discussion of certain of those risks and 
uncertainties and the factors that could cause JPMorgan 
Chase’s actual results to differ materially because of those 
risks and uncertainties.
JPMorgan Chase & Co.  (NYSE: JPM), a financial holding 
company incorporated under Delaware law in 1968, is a 
leading  financial services firm based in the United States of 
America  (“U.S. ”), with operations worldwide.  JPMorgan 
Chase had  $3.7 trillion  in assets and $280.7 billion  in 
stockholders’ equity as of M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1. The Firm is a 
leader in investment banking, financial services for 
consumers and small businesses, commercial  banking, 
financial transaction processing and asset management. 
Under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands, the Firm serves 
millions of customers in the U.S. and globally many of the 
world’s most prominent corporate, institutional and 
government clients.  JPMorgan Chase’s principal bank subsidiary is JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, National Association (“JPMorgan Chase Bank , 
N.A.”), a national banking association with U.S. branches in  
38 states and Washington, D.C. as of  M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1. 
JPMorgan Chase’s principal non-bank subsidiary is J.P. 
Morgan Securities LLC (“J.P. Morgan Securities”), a U.S. 
broker-dealer. The bank and non-bank subsidiaries of 
JPMorgan Chase operate nationally as well as through 
overseas branches and subsidiaries, representative offices 
and subsidiary foreign banks. The Firm’s principal operating 
subsidiary outside the U.S.  is J.P. Morgan Securities plc, a 
U.K.-based subsidiary of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.  
For management reporting purposes, the Firm’s activities 
are organized into four major reportable business 
segments, as well as a Corporate segment. The Firm’s 
consumer business segment is Consumer & Community 
Banking ( “CCB ”). The Firm’s wholesale business segments 
are the Corporate & Investment Bank ( “CIB”), Commercial 
Banking ( “CB”), and Asset & Wealth Management ( “AWM ”). 
Refer to Note 25 of this Form 10-Q and Note 32 of 
JPMorgan Chase’s 2020  Form 10-K for a description of the 
Firm’s business segments and the products and services 
they provide to their respective client bases.
The Firm's website is www.jpmorganchase.com. JPMorgan 
Chase makes available on its website, free of charge, annual 
reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q and 
current reports on Form 8-K pursuant to Section 13(a) or 
Section 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as 
soon as reasonably practicable after it electronically files or 
furnishes such material to the U.S. Securities and Exchange 
Commission (the “SEC”) at www.sec.gov. JPMorgan Chase 
makes important information about the Firm available on 
its website, including the Investor Relations section of its 
website at https://www.jpmorganchase.com/ir.

title: Firmwide overview
heading: Firmwide overview
start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase reported net income of $14.3 billion for the first quarter of 2021 , or $4.50 per share, on net revenue of $32.3 billion.
summary:
- Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for Q1 2021, highlighting selected information and advising readers to consult the full Form 10‑Q and 2020 Form 10‑K for complete context, risks, and critical accounting estimates.
- Firmwide financial results (Q1 2021 vs. Q1 2020):
  - Net income $14.3B, up $11.4B; diluted EPS $4.50, up 477%.
  - Total net revenue $32.3B, up 14%; noninterest revenue up 40% on stronger CIB Markets, higher Investment Banking fees, and absence of prior‑year losses; net interest income down 11% due to lower rates partially offset by balance sheet growth.
  - Noninterest expense $18.7B, up 12%, reflecting higher volume/revenue‑related costs, continued investments, and a $550M contribution to the Firm’s Foundation.
  - Provision for credit losses a net benefit of $4.2B driven by $5.2B allowance reduction, versus an $8.3B expense in prior year tied to a $6.8B allowance build.
  - Pre‑provision profit $13.5B, up 18%.
  - Returns: ROE 23% and ROTCE 29% (up from 4% and 5%).
  - Book value per share $82.31 (up 8%); tangible book value per share $66.56 (up 10%).
- Credit quality and reserves:
  - Total allowance for credit losses $25.6B; allowance for loan losses to retained loans coverage ratio 2.42% (down from 2.95% in Q4 2020; up from 2.32% YoY).
  - Nonperforming assets $10.3B, up $3.2B YoY due to deterioration across multiple wholesale industries and COVID‑19 impacts on consumer loans; down $649M from Dec 31, 2020, on portfolio activity and upgrades (notably Oil & Gas and Individuals) and sales of certain CIB consumer nonaccrual loans at fair value.
- Balance sheet trends:
  - Average loans ~$1.0T, up 1%, with growth in AWM and CIB, partially offset by declines in CCB and CB; PPP originations contributed in CCB and CB.
  - Average deposits ~$2.2T, up 36%, reflecting significant inflows across LOBs primarily from government actions in response to COVID‑19.
- Liquidity and capital:
  - Average eligible HQLA ~$697B; unencumbered marketable securities ~$841B; total liquidity sources ~ $1.5T.
  - Capital ratios (reflecting Federal Reserve COVID‑19 relief and CECL transition): CET1 13.1%, Tier 1 15.0%, Total capital 17.2%.
- Notes:
  - Certain prior‑period amounts revised to conform to current presentation.
  - Comparisons are Q1 2021 vs Q1 2020 unless otherwise specified.
text:
Firmwide overview 
JPMorgan Chase reported net income of $14.3 billion for 
the first quarter of 2021 , or $4.50 per share, on net 
revenue of $32.3 billion. The Firm reported ROE of 23% 
and ROTCE of 29%. The Firm's results for the first quarter 
of 2021 included a reduction in the allowance for credit 
losses of $5.2 billion  compared to an increase in the 
allowance for credit losses of $6.8 billion in the prior year , 
as well as a $550 million contribution to the Firm's 
Foundation.  
•Net income was $14.3 billion, up $11.4 billion.
•Total net revenue was up 14%. Noninterest revenue was 
$19.4 billion, up 40%,  predominantly driven by higher 
CIB Markets revenue, higher Investment Banking fees, 
and the absence of losses in Credit Adjustments and 
Other in CIB and markdowns on held-for-sale positions in 
the bridge financing portfolio in CIB and CB recorded in 
the prior year. Net interest income was $12.9 billion, 
down 11%, predominantly driven by the impact of lower 
rates partially offset by balance sheet growth.   •Noninterest expense was $18.7 billion, up 12%,

title: Business Developments
heading: Business Developments
start_phrase: Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, the Firm has remained focused on serving its clients, customers and communities, as well as the well-being of its employees.
summary:
- The Firm’s COVID-19 response: continued focus on clients, communities, and employee well-being; raised capital and extended credit; active participation in the SBA Paycheck Protection Program with approximately $40 billion funded as of April 30, 2021; ongoing assistance primarily via payment deferrals; majority of employees working from home with health and safety monitoring.
- Regulatory developments tied to COVID-19: overview of U.S. government stimulus measures (CARES Act, Consolidated Appropriations Act, American Rescue Plan Act) supporting consumers, businesses, and loan facilities; references to additional disclosures in the Firm’s 2020 Form 10-K.
- Post-Brexit status: substantial completion of the Firmwide Brexit Implementation program to ensure continuity for EU clients; acknowledgment of the March 26, 2021 U.K.–EU Memorandum of Understanding on regulatory cooperation; ongoing monitoring to maintain business continuity.
- Interbank Offered Rate (IBOR) transition: confirmation of cessation timelines—USD LIBOR principal tenors ending after June 30, 2023, and sterling, yen, Swiss franc, euro LIBOR and certain USD LIBOR tenors ending December 31, 2021; prioritization of contract remediation, risk mitigation activities, and monitoring of U.S. Treasury tax transition relief; references to further details in the 2020 Form 10-K.
text:
Business Developments 
COVID-19 Pandemic
Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, the Firm has remained 
focused on serving its clients, customers and communities, 
as well as the well-being of its employees. 
The Firm has raised capital and provided credit to support 
its customers and clients. The Firm continues to participate 
in the Small Business Association’s (“SBA”) PPP and since 
inception of the Program has  funded approximately $40 
billion as of April 30, 2021. Whi le the Firm’s temporary 
assistance measures for those impacted by the pandemic 
have steadily declined since early 2020, the Firm continues 
to assist those impacted, primarily in the form of payment 
deferrals.
Refer to Credit Portfolio on page 47  for further information 
on PPP; Consumer Credit portfolio on pages 48-52  and 
Wholesale Credit Portfolio on pages 53-62  for further 
information on retained loans under payment deferral. 
Refer to Credit Portfolio on page 113 of JPMorgan Chase's 
2020 Form 10-K for further information on PPP; Consumer 
Credit Portfolio on page 116 and Wholesale Credit Portfolio 
on page 122 of JPMorgan Chase's 2020 Form 10-K for 
further information on retained loans under payment 
deferral.
The Firm remains focused on the well-being of its 
employees. While the vast majority of its global workforce 
continue to work from home, the Firm is actively monitoring 
the health and safety situations at local and regional levels, 
and will adapt its plans as these situations evolve.
Regulatory Developments Relating to the COVID-19 
Pandemic 
To address the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, 
the U.S. government as well as central banks and banking 
authorities around the world have taken and continue to 
take actions to help individuals, households and businesses 
that have been adversely affected by the economic 
disruption caused by the pandemic. In the U.S., several 
stimulus packages were enacted including the CARES Act in 
March of 2020, the Consolidated Appropriations Act in 
December of 2020 and the American Rescue Plan Act in 
March of 2021, which provided funding to support loan 
facilities to assist consumers and businesses and stimulus 
payments to individuals.
Refer to Regulatory Developments Relating to the COVID-19 
Pandemic on pages 52-53 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 
10-K for further discussion on U.S. government actions 
impacting the Firm and U.S. government facilities and 
programs in which the Firm has participated. Post Brexit
Prior to December 31, 2020 the Firm substantially 
completed its Firmwide Brexit Implementation program 
which was intended to ensure the continuity of its business 
and operations with respect to EU clients. On March 26, 
2021, the U.K. and the EU agreed on a Memorandum of 
Understanding that sets out a framework for regulatory 
cooperation in relation to cross-border financial services. 
The Firm will monitor developments and take any necessary 
actions to ensure business continuity with respect to the 
Firm's EU clients. Refer to Business Developments on page 
50 of the 2020 Form 10-K for additional information.
Interbank Offered Rate (“IBOR”) transition
On March 5, 2021, the Financial Conduct Authority 
confirmed that the publication of the principal tenors of 
U.S. dollar LIBOR (i.e., overnight, one-month, three-month, 
six-month and 12-month LIBOR) will cease immediately 
following a final publication on June 30, 2023. The 
scheduled cessation date for U.K. sterling, Japanese yen, 
Swiss franc and Euro LIBOR, and the one-week and two-
month tenors of U.S. dollar LIBOR, remains December 31, 
2021, and the Firm is prioritizing those currencies and 
tenors of LIBOR for contract remediation in 2021.
The Firm continues to make progress on its initiatives to 
appropriately mitigate the risks associated with IBOR 
discontinuation, including contract remediation. The Firm 
also continues to monitor the transition relief being 
considered by the U.S. Treasury Department regarding the 
tax implications of reference rate reform.  Refer to Business 
Developments on page 51 of t he 2020 Form 10-K for a 
discussion of the Firm’s initiatives to address the expected 
discontinuation of the London Interbank Offered Rate 
(“LIBOR”) and other IBORs.
8

summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for the three months ended March 31, 2021 vs. 2020, with cross-references to segment details and critical accounting estimates.
- Total net revenue: Up 14% to $32.3B, driven by a 40% increase in noninterest revenue; net interest income declined 11%.
- Investment banking fees: Up 59% to $3.0B, reflecting stronger equity underwriting (IPOs), increased advisory from more completed deals, and higher debt underwriting (high-yield and leveraged loans) amid higher industry fees and wallet share gains (CIB).
- Principal transactions revenue: Up 121% to $6.5B, aided by absence of two large prior-year losses (CIB Credit Adjustments & Other and bridge financing markdowns). Excluding these, growth came from strong Equity Markets (derivatives, cash equities, prime brokerage) and Fixed Income Markets (securitized products, credit), partly offset by lower Rates and Currencies & EM; also net gains on legacy private equity in Corporate. Note that CIB Markets performance is assessed on total revenue, given offsets with net interest income.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 1%, as lower deposit-related fees in CCB (from higher balances) were largely offset by higher cash management fees in CIB/CB and higher lending-related/commitment fees in CIB.
- Asset management, administration and commissions: Up 11% to $5.0B, driven by higher AWM fees from strong net inflows into long-term and liquidity products and higher market levels (net of liquidity fee waivers), plus higher investment assets in CCB.
- Investment securities gains: Down 94% to $14MM, reflecting portfolio repositioning.
- Mortgage fees and related income: Up 120% to $704MM on higher production margins and volumes (CCB).
- Card income: Up 36% to $1.35B on lower acquisition costs and higher net interchange as debit/credit spend returned to pre-pandemic levels (CCB).
- Other income: Down 10% to $1.12B, due to weather-related write-downs and higher amortization in tax-oriented renewable energy investments (offset in part by related tax credits), lower gains on certain Corporate investments, and lower auto operating lease income in CCB; partially offset by valuation gains in AWM and the absence of prior-year losses on certain CIB equity investments. Footnote notes operating lease income of $1.3B (2021) vs. $1.4B (2020).
- Net interest income: Down 11% to $12.9B, predominantly from lower rates, partly offset by balance sheet growth. Average interest-earning assets rose $661B to $3.1T; yield fell 127 bps to 1.87%. Net yield (FTE) fell 68 bps to 1.69%; excluding CIB Markets, net yield fell 108 bps to 1.93% (non-GAAP measures referenced).
- Provision for credit losses: Swing to a net release of $4.16B vs. an $8.29B build in prior year, driven by reductions in both consumer and wholesale allowances.
  - Consumer: $3.50B net release vs. $5.68B build, reflecting a $4.5B allowance reduction (including $3.5B in Card from improved macroeconomic scenarios and $625MM in Home Lending from improved HPI and portfolio runoff), lower Card net charge-offs helped by payment assistance and government stimulus, and comparison to a $4.4B prior-year build.
  - Wholesale: $671MM net release vs. $2.59B build, reflecting a $716MM allowance reduction on improved macroeconomic scenarios.
- Repeated references to segment-level discussions (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate) and notes for further detail, including non-GAAP reconciliations and credit allowance disclosures.

title: Provision for credit losses
heading: Provision for credit losses
start_phrase: The provision for credit losses decreased driven by net reductions in both the consumer and wholesale allowance for credit losses.
summary:
- Other income decreased, driven by weather-related write-downs and higher amortization on alternative energy investments in CIB (with tax credits reducing tax expense), lower gains on certain Corporate investments, and lower operating lease income in CCB; partially offset by valuation gains in AWM and the absence of prior-year equity investment losses in CIB.
- Net interest income declined primarily due to lower rates, partly offset by balance sheet growth. Average interest-earning assets rose to $3.1 trillion (+$661 billion), with yield down to 1.87% (-127 bps). Net yield on an FTE basis was 1.69% (-68 bps); excluding CIB Markets, 1.93% (-108 bps). These yields are non-GAAP measures with further details referenced.
- Provision for credit losses swung to a net release of $4.2 billion in Q1 2021 versus an $8.3 billion build in Q1 2020. By category: consumer excluding credit card $(984) million, credit card $(2,517) million, total consumer $(3,501) million, wholesale $(671) million, and investment securities $16 million.
- The consumer reserve release reflected a $4.5 billion reduction in allowances (including $3.5 billion in Card on improved macroeconomic scenarios and $625 million in Home Lending on better HPI expectations and portfolio runoff), lower net charge-offs in Card aided by payment assistance and government stimulus, and the absence of a prior-year $4.4 billion addition.
- Wholesale reserves decreased by $716 million across lines of business, reflecting improved macroeconomic scenarios.
- References are provided to segment results, allowance for credit losses, and non-GAAP reconciliations for further detail.

title: Noninterest expense
heading: Noninterest expense
start_phrase: Compensation expense increased predominantly driven by higher revenue- related expense in CIB, as well as the impact of investments in the businesses.
summary:
- Focus: Noninterest expense and income tax expense for the three months ended March 31, 2021 vs. 2020.
- Noninterest expense totaled $18,725 million, up 12% from $16,791 million.
  - Compensation expense: $10,601 million, up 19% (from $8,895 million), driven by higher revenue-related expense in CIB and business investment.
  - Noncompensation expense: $8,124 million, up 3% (from $7,896 million), with components:
    - Occupancy: $1,115 million (+5%)
    - Technology, communications and equipment: $2,519 million (−2%)
    - Professional and outside services: $2,203 million (+9%)
    - Marketing: $751 million (−6%)
    - Other expense: $1,536 million (+8%)
  - Included in other: Firmwide legal expense of $28 million (2021) vs. $197 million (2020); FDIC-related expense of $201 million (2021) vs. $99 million (2020).
  - Drivers of noncompensation change: higher contribution expense (including a $550 million donation of equity investments to the Firm’s Foundation), increased business/technology investment, and higher FDIC-related expense from balance sheet growth; partially offset by lower legal expense (mainly in CIB) and lower structural costs (e.g., travel and entertainment, operating losses).
  - Other volume- and revenue-related expense was flat: higher brokerage expense in CIB and distribution expense in AWM offset by lower depreciation from reduced auto lease assets in CCB.
- Income tax expense:
  - Income before tax: $17,697 million vs. $3,210 million (+451%).
  - Income tax expense: $3,397 million vs. $345 million (not meaningful comparison).
  - Effective tax rate: 19.2% vs. 10.7%; increase driven by higher pre-tax income (reducing relative impact of certain tax benefits) and the resolution of certain tax audits.
  - Note: prior-period amounts revised to conform with current presentation.

title: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
heading: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 0.
summary:
- Scope: Analysis of significant changes in the consolidated balance sheet between March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, highlighting key asset, liability, and equity movements and their business drivers.
- Scale: Total assets up 9% to $3.69T; total liabilities up 10% to $3.41T; stockholders’ equity flat at ~$281B.
- Assets:
  - Cash and due from banks and deposits with banks up (cash/deposits with central banks) due to strong deposit growth and fewer opportunities to deploy in reverse repos.
  - Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements down on lower Treasury/CIO deployment and reduced CIB market-making, partly offset by higher demand to cover short positions.
  - Securities borrowed up on client-driven financing and short-cover demand in CIB prime brokerage/markets.
  - Trading assets up on strong client-driven equity market-making, including prime brokerage.
  - Investment securities slightly higher: net HTM U.S. Treasury purchases offset by AFS declines from paydowns and valuation losses (partly offset by net purchases).
  - Loans flat: seasonal/card paydowns, lower CB loans, and Home Lending paydowns offset by PPP originations (CBB/CB), CIB loans held-for-sale/at fair value, and AWM securities-based/custom lending and mortgages.
  - Allowance for loan losses down 19% ($28.3B to $23.0B): $4.5B reduction in consumer (card; residential real estate aided by improved HPI and runoff) and $875MM net reduction in wholesale on improved macro scenarios; $107MM added to allowance for lending-related commitments; net ACL reduction of $5.2B.
  - Accrued interest and receivables up on higher CIB prime brokerage client receivables.
  - Goodwill/MSRs/other intangibles up on higher MSRs (slower prepayments with higher rates) and net additions.
  - Other assets up on securities financing in CIB prime brokerage and higher CCP cash collateral.
- Liabilities:
  - Deposits up 6% across LOBs, driven by government actions tied to COVID-19, lower spending, and account growth (consumer/small business).
  - Federal funds purchased and repos up 41% from higher secured financing of AFS in Treasury/CIO, higher CIB trading assets, and client activity.
  - Short-term borrowings up 22% from prime brokerage financing, net issuance of CIB structured notes, and Treasury/CIO commercial paper issuance.
  - Trading liabilities up 12% on client-driven Fixed Income market-making (higher short positions), partly offset by lower derivative payables.
  - Accounts payable and other liabilities up 23% due to CIB prime brokerage securities financing.
  - Beneficial interests in consolidated VIEs down 11% on lower issuances tied to reduced multi-seller conduit loan balances.
  - Long-term debt roughly flat (maturities and higher-rate hedge adjustments offset by net issuance).
- Equity and AOCI:
  - Stockholders’ equity flat as net income was offset by capital actions and lower AOCI; AOCI decline driven by higher rates impacting AFS securities and cash flow hedges.
- Themes and references:
  - Liquidity deployment shifted toward central bank deposits; elevated client-driven prime brokerage and market-making activity influenced multiple line items.
  - Improved macroeconomic outlook drove sizeable reserve releases.
  - Multiple cross-references to Liquidity, Credit and Investment Risk Management, and relevant financial statement notes.

title: Consolidated cash flows analysis
heading: Consolidated cash flows analysis
start_phrase: The following is a discussion of cash flow activities during the three months ended M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1 and 2020 .
summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated cash flows for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020, highlighting sources and uses of cash across operating, investing, and financing activities.
- Key totals (in millions): Operating activities used $43,872 in 2021 vs. $120,089 in 2020; Investing activities provided $15,391 in 2021 vs. used $135,833 in 2020; Financing activities provided $218,911 in 2021 vs. $362,305 in 2020; Effect of exchange rates was $(6,967) in 2021 vs. $(2,480) in 2020; Net increase in cash and due from banks and deposits with banks was $183,463 in 2021 vs. $103,903 in 2020.
- Operating activities drivers:
  - 2021: Cash used due to higher trading assets, accrued interest and accounts receivable, and securities borrowed; partially offset by higher accounts payable and other liabilities and lower other assets.
  - 2020: Cash used due to higher trading assets, other assets, and accrued interest and accounts receivable; partially offset by higher trading liabilities and higher accounts payable and other liabilities.
- Investing activities drivers:
  - 2021: Cash provided by lower securities purchased under resale agreements and net proceeds from sales and securitizations of loans held-for-investment; partially offset by net purchases of investment securities.
  - 2020: Cash used for net purchases of investment securities, net loan originations, and purchases of assets from money market mutual fund clients under the FRBB’s MMLF.
- Financing activities drivers:
  - 2021 and 2020: Cash provided by higher deposits, increased securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements, and net proceeds from long- and short-term borrowings; cash used for share repurchases and dividends on common and preferred stock in both periods.
- References to additional detail in the Form 10-Q (Consolidated Balance Sheets Analysis; Capital Risk Management; Liquidity Risk Management) and the 2020 Form 10-K for broader context on cash flow drivers.

title: OFF-BALANCE SHEET ARRANGEMENTS
heading: OFF-BALANCE SHEET ARRANGEMENTS
start_phrase: In the normal course of business, the Firm enters into various off-balance sheet arrangements and contractual obligations that may require future cash payments.
summary:
- Outlines the firm’s use of off-balance sheet arrangements and contractual obligations that may require future cash payments, noting that some obligations are recorded on-balance sheet while others are disclosed off-balance sheet under U.S. GAAP.
- Highlights special-purpose entities (SPEs), which are a type of variable interest entity (VIE), and lending-related financial instruments (e.g., commitments and guarantees) as key off-balance sheet structures.
- States the firm holds capital against exposures arising from SPE-related transactions, including derivative contracts and lending-related commitments and guarantees.
- Confirms the firm has no commitments to issue its own stock to support any SPE transactions and requires all SPE transactions to be at arm’s length and reflect market pricing.
- Provides a disclosure index within the Form 10-Q:
  - Note 13 (pages 137–142): Variable interests and other obligations from nonconsolidated VIEs.
  - Note 22 (pages 152–155): Off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments.
  - Refers to Note 1 for consolidation policies.
text:
OFF-BALANCE SHEET ARRANGEMENTS
In the normal course of business, the Firm enters into various off-balance sheet arrangements and contractual obligations that 
may require future cash payments. Certain obligations are recognized on-balance sheet, while others are disclosed as off-
balance sheet under accounting principles generally accepted in the U.S. (“U.S. GAAP”). 
Special-purpose entities
The Firm has several types of off–balance sheet arrangements, including through nonconsolidated special-purpose entities 
(“SPEs”), which are a type of VIE, and through lending-related financial instruments (e.g., commitments and guarantees). 
The Firm holds capital, as appropriate, against all SPE-related transactions and related exposures, such as derivative contracts 
and lending-related commitments and guarantees.
The Firm has no commitments to issue its own stock to support any SPE transaction, and its policies require that transactions 
with SPEs be conducted at arm’s length and reflect market pricing.

title: EXPLANATION AND RECONCILIATION OF THE FIRM’S USE OF NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES
heading: EXPLANATION AND RECONCILIATION OF THE FIRM’S USE OF NON-GAAP FINANCIAL MEASURES
start_phrase: The Firm prepares its Consolidated Financial Statements in accordance with U.S. GAAP and this presentation is referred to as “reported” basis; these financial statements appear on pages 79-83 .
summary:
- Explains JPMorgan Chase’s use of non-GAAP financial measures alongside U.S. GAAP (“reported”) results and why management reviews them.
- Defines key non-GAAP measures used firmwide/segment-level: managed (FTE) basis results and overhead ratio; pre-provision profit; net interest income (NII) and net yield excluding CIB Markets; tangible common equity (TCE), return on TCE (ROTCE), and tangible book value per share (TBVPS); and allowance for loan losses to loans retained (excluding trade finance and conduits).
- Provides a reconciliation from reported GAAP to managed (FTE) basis for Q1 2021 and Q1 2020, showing:
  - FTE adjustments that increase total net revenue and pre-tax income (e.g., $853mm in Q1’21; $724mm in Q1’20), with no change to net income.
  - Overhead ratio modestly lower on a managed basis (57% vs 58% reported in Q1’21; 58% vs 59% in Q1’20).
  - Notes that prior-period amounts were revised and that FTE adjustments are predominantly in CIB, CB, and Corporate.
- Details NII and net yield excluding CIB Markets for Q1 2021 vs Q1 2020:
  - NII (managed) down 11%; excluding CIB Markets down 17%.
  - CIB Markets NII up 39%.
  - Average interest-earning assets materially higher; yields declined (managed yield 1.69% vs 2.37%; ex-CIB yield 1.93% vs 3.01%).
- Reconciles common stockholders’ equity to TCE at period-end and on average:
  - Subtracts goodwill and other intangibles; adds certain deferred tax liabilities.
  - Reports TCE levels, TBVPS ($66.56 at 3/31/21 vs $66.11 at 12/31/20), and ROTCE (29% in Q1’21 vs 5% in Q1’20).
- References JPMorgan Chase 2020 Form 10-K (pages 62–64) for further discussion of non-GAAP and key performance measures.

title: Description of business segment reporting methodology
heading: Description of business segment reporting methodology
start_phrase: Results of the business segments are intended to present each segment as if it were a stand-alone business.
summary:
- The firm reports and manages performance by line of business, with four major reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management—plus a Corporate segment.
- Segments are defined by products/services or customer type and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates financial information.
- Results are presented on a managed (non-GAAP) basis; references are provided for the definition and reconciliations.
- Segment reporting methodology presents each LOB as a stand‑alone business, allocating certain income and expense items; assumptions, methodologies, and classifications are reviewed and refined periodically.
- The firm assesses capital needs for each LOB at least annually and provides business metrics used by management, investors, and analysts to evaluate performance.
- Revenue sharing: when multiple segments collaborate on client transactions, revenue is recognized by the segment owning the product/service with allocations to participating segments; segment results reflect these agreements.
- Capital allocation: equity is assigned to each segment; allocation methodologies are periodically reassessed and may change LOB capital levels; additional details and references to the 2020 Form 10‑K are provided.
text:
Description of business segment reporting methodology
Results of the business segments are intended to present 
each segment as if it were a stand-alone business. The 
management reporting process that derives business 
segment results includes the allocation of certain income 
and expense items. The Firm periodically assesses the 
assumptions, methodologies and reporting classifications 
used for segment reporting, and further refinements may 
be implemented in future periods. The Firm also assesses 
the level of capital required for each LOB on at least an 
annual basis. The Firm’s LOBs also provide various business 
metrics which are utilized by the Firm and its investors and 
analysts in assessing performance. Revenue sharing 
When business segments join efforts to sell products and 
services to the Firm’s clients, the participating business 
segments may agree to share revenue from those 
transactions. Revenue is generally recognized in the 
segment responsible for the related product or service, with 
allocations to the other segment(s) involved in the 
transaction. The segment results reflect these revenue-
sharing agreements.
Capital allocation
The amount of capital assigned to each segment  is referred 
to as equity. Periodically, the assumptions and 
methodologies used to allocate capital are assessed and as 
a result, the capital allocated to the LOBs may change. 
Refe r to Line of business equity on  page 39 , and  page 98  of 
JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K for additional 
information on capital allocation.

segment reporting methodology on pages 65–66  of

of those methodologies.

summary:
- Purpose: Presents managed-basis segment results for the Firm for the three months ended March 31, 2021 versus 2020, including revenue, expenses, pre-provision profit, credit loss provisions, net income, and ROE; notes that a comparative discussion by segment follows.

- Consumer & Community Banking (CCB):
  - Revenue down 6% to $12.5B; expenses roughly flat (-1%).
  - Large provision release (-$3.6B vs +$5.8B prior) drove net income to $6.7B (from $0.2B); ROE 54% (vs 1%).
  - Pre-provision profit declined 12% to $5.3B.

- Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB):
  - Revenue up 46% to $14.6B; expenses up 19%.
  - Pre-provision profit up 85% to $7.5B; provision release (-$331MM vs +$1.4B).
  - Net income $5.7B, up 189%; ROE 27% (vs 9%).

- Commercial Banking (CB):
  - Revenue up 11% to $2.4B; expenses down 2%.
  - Pre-provision profit up 21% to $1.4B; provision release (-$118MM vs +$1.0B).
  - Net income $1.17B vs $139MM; ROE 19% (vs 2%).

- Asset & Wealth Management (AWM):
  - Revenue up 20% to $4.1B; expenses up 6%.
  - Pre-provision profit up 58% to $1.5B; provision release (-$121MM vs +$94MM).
  - Net income $1.24B, up 86%; ROE 35% (vs 25%).

- Corporate:
  - Revenue negative (-$473MM vs +$166MM); expenses up sharply to $876MM.
  - Pre-provision loss of $1.35B (vs $20MM profit); provision modestly higher.
  - Net loss of $580MM (vs $125MM loss); ROE not meaningful.

- Total Firm:
  - Revenue up 14% to $33.1B; expenses up 12% to $18.7B.
  - Pre-provision profit up 18% to $14.4B.
  - Credit provision swung to a $4.16B release (from an $8.29B build).
  - Net income $14.3B, up 399%; ROE 23% (vs 4%).

- Key theme: Broad-based earnings improvement driven by strong revenue growth in markets/investment banking and substantial credit reserve releases across most segments compared with prior-year builds; Corporate segment posted a larger loss.

Expenses were $7.2B (flat; includes $916MM leased asset depreciation). Revenue by line: Consumer & Business Banking $5.64B (-10%), Home Lending $1.46B (+26%), Card & Auto $5.42B (-7%); mortgage fees totaled $703MM (+120%) with production revenue $757MM and net servicing revenue -$54MM (MSR risk management -$115MM). Period-end balances: deposits $1.04T (+32%), total loans $431.6B (-4%) including CBB $52.7B (with $23.4B PPP), Home Lending $178.8B (-13%), Card $132.5B (-14%), Auto $67.7B (+10%); equity $50B; headcount 126,084. Credit metrics: nonaccrual loans $5.67B (+41%; excludes certain government-insured and COVID deferral impacts), total net charge-offs $1.02B (-22%) with rates of 2.97% Card, 0.53% CBB (PPP SBA-guaranteed), 0.16% Auto, and -0.12% Home Lending; 30+ day delinquency rates improved (Home 1.07%, Card 1.40%, Auto 0.42%); allowance for loan losses $17.45B (-7%; Card $14.30B, Home $1.24B, Auto $0.89B, CBB $1.02B). Financial ratios: ROE 54%, overhead ratio 58. Credit Adjustments & Other recorded a small $3 million loss versus a $951 million loss in the prior year (which was largely due to funding spread widening on derivatives).

Provision for credit losses was a net benefit of $331 million, reflecting a reduction in the allowance for credit losses, compared with a $1.4 billion expense in the prior year.

- Average balances: Total assets increased 20% to $1.294 trillion. Trading assets (debt and equity) rose 17% to $465 billion; derivative receivables increased 41% to $78 billion. Average total loans were up 11% to $182 billion (retained +6%; HFS/at FV +30%). Headcount rose 4% to 62,772.
- Credit quality and reserves: Net recoveries of $7 million versus net charge-offs of $55 million in the prior year. Nonperforming assets increased 57% to $2.49 billion, including total nonaccrual loans up 45% to $2.11 billion and derivative receivables of $284 million. Key ratios: net charge-off rate of -0.02%; allowance to loans retained 1.48% (2.06% excluding trade finance and conduits); nonaccrual loans to total loans 1.17%.
- Investment banking fees: Total fees surged 57% to $2.99 billion, with advisory up 35% to $680 million, equity underwriting up 219% to $1.06 billion, and debt underwriting up 17% to $1.25 billion.

summary:
- Scope: Quarterly results summary for JPMorgan Chase’s Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) for Q1 2021 vs Q1 2020, with references to the 2020 Form 10-K and risk management sections.
- Performance highlights:
  - Net income: $1.244B, up 86%.

    - Net interest income: $931M, up 8%.
    - Noninterest revenue: $3.146B, up 24% (asset management, administration and commissions $2.888B, up 12%; all other income $258M vs a loss prior year).

  - Global Private Bank: $1.892B, up 15%, driven by higher deposit and loan balances, higher asset management fees, loan margin expansion, and an investment valuation gain, partially offset by deposit margin compression.
- Profitability ratios:
  - Return on equity: 35% (vs 25%).

title: FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT - Introduction
heading: FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT
start_phrase: Risk is an inherent part of JPMorgan Chase’s business activities.
summary: Introduction to JPMorgan Chase’s firmwide risk management outlines that risk is inherent across activities such as consumer and wholesale lending, investment advice, market-making, and other products/services, with an objective to balance client, customer, and investor interests while protecting the Firm’s safety and soundness. It specifies core requirements for effective risk management: firmwide responsibility for identifying and escalating risks, Line of Business and Corporate ownership of risk identification, assessment, data, and management, and structured risk governance. It also ties risk management to a disciplined, balanced compensation framework with strong internal governance and independent oversight by the Board of Directors, where risk and control issues are factored into performance evaluations and incentive compensation.
text:
FIRMWIDE RISK MANAGEMENT 
Risk is an inherent part of JPMorgan Chase’s business 
activities. When the Firm extends a consumer or wholesale 
loan, advises customers and clients on their investment 
decisions, makes markets in securities, or offers other 
products or services, the Firm takes on some degree of risk. 
The Firm’s overall objective is to manage its businesses, and 
the associated risks, in a manner that balances serving the 
interests of its clients, customers and investors and protects 
the safety and soundness of the Firm.  
The Firm believes that effective risk management requires, 
among other things: 
•Acceptance of responsibility, including identification and 
escalation of risks by all individuals within the Firm; 
•Ownership of risk identification, assessment, data and 
management within each of the LOBs and Corporate; and 
•Firmwide structures for risk governance. 
The Firm follows a disciplined and balanced compensation 
framework with strong internal governance and 
independent oversight by the Board of Directors (the 
“Board”). The impact of risk and control issues is carefully 
considered in the Firm’s performance evaluation and 
incentive compensation processes.

Effective risk management is defined by three pillars: individual accountability for identifying and escalating risks; ownership of risk identification, assessment, data, and management within each line of business and Corporate; and firmwide governance structures. It highlights a disciplined compensation framework with strong internal governance and independent Board oversight, where risk and control outcomes factor into performance evaluations and incentives. The risk governance and oversight framework focuses on understanding risk drivers, types, and impacts, and provides cross-references to detailed discussions in the Firm’s Form 10-Q and 2020 Form 10-K. The specific risk areas covered include:
- Strategic risk

- Consumer credit risk
- Wholesale credit risk
- Investment portfolio risk
- Market risk
- Country risk
- Operational risk

title: Basel III Overview
heading: Basel III Overview
start_phrase: The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and internationally active U.S. Bank Holding Companies ("BHCs") and banks, including the Firm and its insured depository institution (“IDI”) subsidiaries, including JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
summary:
- Defines capital risk as the possibility that the Firm’s capital level or composition is insufficient to support its activities and risks in normal and stressed conditions; notes COVID-19 impacts but that the Firm remains well-capitalized.
- Points to additional disclosures in the 2020 Form 10-K, this Form 10-Q, and Pillar 3 reports for capital planning and stress testing details.
- Outlines Basel III framework: capital requirements based on risk-weighted assets (RWA) using two methods—Standardized and Advanced—and capital adequacy assessed against the more binding of the two.
- States the Firm’s Basel III Standardized risk-based ratios are currently more binding than the Advanced approach.
- Notes Advanced Approach institutions must calculate the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR).
- Describes CECL regulatory capital transition: optional two-year delay beginning Jan 1, 2020 with a three-year phase-in from Jan 1, 2022; the Firm elected this, excluding $4.5B from capital metrics as of Mar 31, 2021 ($2.7B day-one retained earnings impact plus 25% of a $7.0B allowance increase). These effects flow through Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
- Details temporary SLR relief: from Apr 1, 2020 to Mar 31, 2021, BHCs could exclude on-balance sheet U.S. Treasuries and Federal Reserve Bank deposits from total leverage exposure; IDI subsidiaries had an optional exclusion under a parallel rule. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. did not elect the IDI exclusion.
- Explains PPP capital treatment: zero percent risk weight applied to PPP loans, limiting impact on risk-based ratios; Firm held about $32B of PPP loans as of Mar 31, 2021 and does not expect material credit losses due to SBA guarantees. PPP loans remain in SLR exposure because the Firm did not use the PPPL Facility.
- Summarizes TLAC holdings rule effective Apr 1, 2021: expands capital deduction treatment to holdings of TLAC debt of systemically important banks; not expected to materially affect the Firm’s risk-based capital metrics.
text:
Basel III Overview
The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital 
ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and 
internationally active U.S.  Bank Holding Companies 
("BHCs") and banks, including the Firm and its insured 
depository institution (“IDI”) subsidiaries,  including 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. The minimum amount of 
regulatory capital that must be held by BHCs and banks is 
determined by calculating risk-weighted assets (“RWA”), 
which are on-balance sheet assets and off-balance sheet 
exposures, weighted according to risk. Two comprehensive 
approaches are prescribed for calculating RWA: a 
standardized approach (“Basel III Standardized”), and an 
advanced approach (“Basel III Advanced”). For each of the 
risk-based capital ratios, the capital adequacy of the Firm is 
evaluated against the lower of the Standardized or 
Advanced approac hes compared to their respective 
minimum capital ratios.  
The Firm’s Basel III Standardized-risk-based ratios are 
currently more binding than the Basel III Advanced-risk-
based ratios.  
Basel III also includes a requirement for Advanced 
Approach banking organizations, including the Firm, to 
calculate the  SLR. Refer to SLR o n page 39  for additional 
information.

title: Key Regulatory Developments
heading: Key Regulatory Developments
start_phrase: As part of their response to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the federal banking agencies issued a final rule that provided the option beginning January 1, 2020 to delay the effects of CECL on regulatory capital for two years, followed by a three-year transition period beginning January 1, 2022 (“CECL capital transition provisions”).
summary:
- Defines capital risk as insufficient capital level/composition to support business and risks in normal and stressed environments; notes COVID-19 impacts but that the Firm remained well-capitalized; references 2020 Form 10-K, this 10-Q Note 21, and Pillar 3 reports for more detail.
- Basel III overview:
  - Regulatory capital based on risk-weighted assets (RWA) using two methods: Basel III Standardized and Basel III Advanced.
  - The Firm’s capital adequacy is assessed against the lower (more binding) of the two; currently the Standardized approach is more binding.
  - Advanced Approach firms, including the Firm, must also calculate the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR).
- Key regulatory developments:
  - CECL regulatory capital transition: optional two-year delay plus three-year phase-in; the Firm elected the transition, excluding $4.5 billion from capital metrics as of March 31, 2021 (comprising the $2.7 billion day 1 retained earnings impact and 25% of the $7.0 billion increase in the allowance for credit losses, excluding PCD loans). Effects incorporated into Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
  - Temporary SLR revision: from April 1, 2020 to March 31, 2021, BHCs could exclude on-balance-sheet U.S. Treasuries and Federal Reserve deposits from total leverage exposure; the Firm applied this at the holding company level. An IDI-level option was also provided for the same period, which JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. did not elect.
  - Paycheck Protection Program (PPP): zero percent risk weight applied to PPP loans for risk-based capital; Firm held about $32 billion of PPP loans as of March 31, 2021 and does not expect material credit losses due to SBA guarantees. PPP loans are included in total leverage exposure since the Firm did not use the Federal Reserve’s PPPL Facility.
  - TLAC Holdings rule: effective April 1, 2021; extends capital deduction treatment to holdings of TLAC debt of systemically important banks; not expected to materially impact the Firm’s risk-based capital metrics.
- Capital metrics (March 31, 2021 vs. December 31, 2020), reflecting CECL transition and PPP zero risk weight:
  - CET1 capital: $206.1B (vs. $205.1B).
  - RWA: $1.577T Standardized (vs. $1.561T); $1.504T Advanced (vs. $1.484T).
  - Ratios (Standardized; Advanced): CET1 13.1%; 13.7–13.8; Tier 1 15.0%; 15.8; Total capital 17.2–17.3; 17.2–17.3. Minimum requirements including buffers shown for comparison (e.g., CET1 mins approx. 11.3% Standardized; 10.5% Advanced).
  - Leverage-based: Tier 1 leverage ratio 6.7% (vs. 7.0%; minimum 4.0%). SLR 6.7% (vs. 6.9%; minimum 5.0%) with temporary relief; without relief, SLR would be 5.5% (vs. 5.8%).
- Emphasizes that Standardized risk-based ratios are the binding constraint and that temporary COVID-related regulatory adjustments (CECL transition and SLR relief) and PPP capital treatment affected reported capital and leverage measures.
text:
Key Regulatory Developments
CECL regulatory capital transition delay . As part of their 
response to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the 
federal banking agencies issued a final rule that provided 
the option beginning January 1, 2020 to delay the effects of 
CECL on regulatory capital for two years, followed by a 
three-year transition period beginning January 1, 2022  
(“CECL capital transition provisions”).  
The Firm has elected to apply the CECL capital transition 
provisions, and accordingly, for the period ended March 31, 
2021, the capital metrics of  the Firm exclude $4.5 billion , 
which is the $2.7 billion  day 1 impact to retained earnings 
and 25% of the $7.0 billion  increase in the allowance for 
credit losses  from January 1, 2020 (excluding allowances 
on PCD loans).   The impacts of the CECL capital transition provisions have 
also been incorporated into Tier 2 capital, adjusted average 
assets, and total leverage exposure.  Refer to Capital Risk 
Management on pages 91-101 and Note 1 of JPMorgan 
Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K for further information on CECL 
capital transition provisions and the CECL accounting 
guidance.  
SLR temporary revision.  The Federal Reserve issued an 
interim final rule that requires, on a temporary basis, the 
calculation of total leverage exposure for purposes of 
calculating the SLR for bank holding companies, to exclude 
the on-balance sheet amounts of U.S. Treasury securities 
and deposits at Federal Reserve Banks. These exclusions 
became effective April 1, 2020, and remained in effect 
through March 31, 2021.   
On June 1, 2020, the Federal Reserve, Office of the 
Comptroller of the Currency (" OCC") and FDIC  issued an 
interim final rule  which became effective April 1, 2020  and 
remained in effect through March 31, 2021 that provides 
IDI subsidiaries with an option to apply this temporary 
exclusion subject to certain restrictions. As of March 31, 
2021, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. did not elect to apply this 
exclusion.
PPP. On April 13, 2020, the federal banking agencies issued 
an interim final rule (issued as final on September 29, 
2020) to neutralize the regulatory capital effects of 
participating in the PPP on risk-based capital ratios by 
applying a zero percent ris k weight to loans originated 
under the program. Given that PPP loans are guaranteed by 
the SBA, the Firm does not expect to realize material credit 
losses on these loans. As of March 31, 2021, the Firm had 
approximately $32 billion of loans under the program.  
Total leverage exposure for purposes of calculating the SLR 
includes PPP loans as the Firm did not participate in the 
Federal Reserve’s Paycheck Protection Program Lending 
(“PPPL”) Facility, which would allow the Firm to exclude 
them under the final rule.  
TLAC Holdings rule . On October 20, 2020, the federal 
bank ing agencies issued a final rule prescribing the 
regulatory capital treatment for holdings of Total Loss-
Absorbing Capacity ("TLAC") debt instruments by certain 
large banking organizations, such as the Firm and JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, N.A. This rule expands the scope of the existing 
capital deductions rule around the holdings of capital 
instruments of financial institutions to also include TLAC 
debt instruments issued by systemically important banking 
organizations. The final rule became effective April 1, 2021 
and is not  expected to have  a material impact on the Firm’s 
risk-based capital metrics.

summary:

- RWA rollforward: Under Basel III Standardized, total RWA rose from $1,560.6B to $1,577.0B (+$16.4B), driven mainly by increases in portfolio levels (+$18.7B; credit +$13.9B, market +$4.8B), partially offset by model/data changes in market risk (−$1.1B) and credit portfolio runoff (−$1.2B). Under Basel III Advanced, total RWA rose from $1,484.4B to $1,503.8B (+$19.4B), with increases across credit (+$11.4B), market (+$4.6B), and operational risk (+$5.1B), offset by market risk model/data changes (−$1.1B) and modest credit portfolio runoff (−$0.7B). Footnotes indicate model/data changes reflect methodology updates per regulatory guidance; portfolio runoff primarily reflects roll-offs in Home Lending; and portfolio level movements (inclusive of rule changes) reflect changes in book size/composition/credit quality/market movements, market risk positions and market moves, operational risk cumulative losses, and certain deductions for excess eligible credit reserves.

- Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR): Tier 1 capital was $237.3B. Total leverage exposure was $3,522.6B after adjustments, including off-balance-sheet exposures and exclusions for U.S. Treasuries and Federal Reserve Bank deposits. - Capital actions: The quarterly common dividend is $0.90 per share, subject to Board approval. Share repurchases, suspended in March 2020 due to COVID-19 and later restricted by the Federal Reserve, resumed in Q1 2021 under a new $30B authorization, with combined dividends and net repurchases capped by the average of the prior four quarters’ net income; these restrictions were extended at least through Q2 2021.

title: LCR and HQLA
heading: LCR and HQLA
start_phrase: The LCR rule requires that the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. maintain an amount of eligible HQLA that is sufficient to meet their respective estimated total net cash outflows over a prospective 30 calendar-day period of significant stress.
summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and directs readers to the 2020 Form 10-K and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for fuller discussion.
- Explains LCR and HQLA requirements: both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must maintain at least 100% LCR; excess HQLA at the bank that isn’t transferable to non‑bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
- Provides average LCR metrics for the three months ended March 31, 2021, December 31, 2020, and March 31, 2020:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: LCR 110% (Mar-21 and Dec-20; 114% Mar-20); HQLA composed of eligible cash and securities; net excess eligible HQLA ~$62–66B.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 166% (Mar-21), 160% (Dec-20), 117% (Mar-20); net excess eligible HQLA rose to ~$443B.
- Notes drivers of change:
  - Firm’s YoY LCR decrease due mainly to higher net cash outflows stemming from significant deposit growth.
  - Bank’s LCR increase driven by deposit growth, largely from government actions related to COVID‑19; this excess liquidity at the bank is excluded from the Firm’s LCR.
  - LCR fluctuates with changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows from business activity.
- Identifies other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities with fair value of ~$841B (Mar-21) vs ~$740B (Dec-20), reflecting higher CIB trading assets and bank excess HQLA from increased deposits.
  - Available borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window of ~$301B (Mar-21) vs ~$307B (Dec-20); noted as available but not viewed as a primary liquidity source.
- Outlines NSFR:
  - Final U.S. NSFR rule effective July 1, 2021; minimum NSFR of 100%; semiannual public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR begins in 2023.
  - The Firm estimates it is compliant with the 100% NSFR requirement.
text:
LCR and HQLA
The LCR rule requires that the Firm and JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A. maintain an amount of eligible  HQLA that is 
sufficient to meet their respective estimated total net cash 
outflows over a prospective 30 calendar-day period of 
significant stress.  Under the LCR rule, the amount of eligible 
HQLA held by  JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. that is in excess of 
its stand-alone 100% minimum LCR requirement, and that is 
not transferable to non-bank affiliates, must be excluded 
from the Firm’s reported eligible HQLA.  The LCR  for both the 
Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is required to be a 
minimum of 100%.  Refer to page 103  of JPMorgan Chase’s 
2020 Form 10-K and the Firm’s U.S. LCR Disclosure reports 
for additional information on HQLA and net cash outflows.

title: Other liquidity sources
heading: Other liquidity sources
start_phrase: In addition to the assets reported in the Firm’s eligible HQLA above, the Firm had unencumbered marketable securities, such as equity and debt securities, that the Firm believes would be available to raise liquidity.
summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and references JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for broader context on the Firm’s Liquidity Risk Management.
- Explains LCR and HQLA requirements: Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must each maintain eligible HQLA sufficient to cover 30-day stressed net cash outflows with a minimum LCR of 100%; surplus HQLA at the bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
- Provides LCR metrics:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co. average LCR: 110% (Q1 2021), 110% (Q4 2020), 114% (Q1 2020).
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. average LCR: 166% (Q1 2021), 160% (Q4 2020), 117% (Q1 2020).
- Details HQLA composition and amounts for the Firm:
  - Eligible cash at central banks: $578.0B (Q1 2021), $455.6B (Q4 2020), $205.0B (Q1 2020).
  - Eligible securities (predominantly U.S. Treasuries, GSE/agency MBS, sovereigns): $118.5B, $241.4B, $343.1B.
  - Total HQLA: $696.6B, $697.1B, $548.2B.
  - Net cash outflows: $634.2B, $634.0B, $482.4B.
  - Net excess eligible HQLA: $62.4B, $63.0B, $65.8B.
  - Bank’s net excess eligible HQLA: $442.6B, $401.9B, $87.1B.
- Notes drivers of changes:
  - Firm’s LCR decreased versus prior year due to higher deposits increasing net cash outflows.
  - Bank’s LCR increased versus both Q4 2020 and Q1 2020 due to deposit growth, largely from government actions related to COVID-19.
  - Excess liquidity at the bank is excluded from the Firm’s LCR under the rule.
  - The Firm’s average LCR fluctuates with changes in HQLA and estimated net cash outflows from ongoing business activity.
- Describes other liquidity sources beyond eligible HQLA:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities with fair value of approximately $841B (Mar 31, 2021) and $740B (Dec 31, 2020); increase driven by higher CIB trading assets and excess eligible HQLA at the bank from deposit growth; actual liquidity raised would depend on market conditions.
  - Available borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window of about $301B (Mar 31, 2021) and $307B (Dec 31, 2020); excludes benefits from HQLA or other unencumbered securities already pledged; not considered a primary liquidity source.
- Introduces NSFR requirements:
  - Final U.S. NSFR rule (issued Oct 20, 2020) effective July 1, 2021; requires at least 100% NSFR on an ongoing basis.
  - Public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR will be required semi-annually beginning in 2023.
  - The Firm estimates it is compliant with the 100% minimum NSFR based on its current understanding of the final rule.
text:
Other liquidity sources
In addition to the assets reported in the Firm’s eligible HQLA 
above, the Firm had unencumbered marketable securities, 
such as equity and debt securities, that the Firm believes 
would be available to raise liquidity. This includes securities 
included as part of the excess eligible HQLA at JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, N.A. that are not transferable to non-bank 
affiliates. The fair value of these securities was approximately 
$841 billion  and $740 billion  as of M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1 and 
D e c e m b e r   3 1 ,  2 0 2 0, respectively , although the amount of 
liquidity that could be raised would be dependent on 
prevailing market conditions. The fair value increased 
compared to December 31, 20 20, primarily due to an 
increase in CIB trading assets and an increase in excess 
eligible HQLA at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. which was 
primarily a result of increased deposits.
The Firm also had available borrowing capacity at  the Federal 
Home Loan Banks (" FHLBs ") and the discount window at the 
Federal Reserve Bank as a result of collateral pledged by the 
Firm to such banks of approximately  $301 billion  and $307 
billion  as of  M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1 and D e c e m b e r   3 1 ,  2 0 2 0, 
respectively. This borrowing capacity excludes the benefit of 
cash and securities reported in the Firm’s eligible HQLA or 
other unencumbered securities that are currently pledged at 
the Federal Reserve Bank discount window and other central 
banks.  Although available, the Firm does not view this 
borrowing capacity at the Federal Reserve Bank discount 
window and the other central banks as a primary source of 
liquidity.

title: NSFR
heading: NSFR
start_phrase: The net stable funding ratio (“NSFR”) is a liquidity requirement for large banking organizations that is intended to measure the adequacy of “available” and “required” amounts of stable funding over a one-year horizon.
summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and directs readers to JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K and U.S. LCR disclosures for more detail.
- Explains LCR and HQLA requirements: both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must maintain at least 100% LCR; excess HQLA at the bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
- Summarizes average LCR metrics for the three months ended March 31, 2021, December 31, 2020, and March 31, 2020:
  - Firm: LCR 110% for Mar-21 and Dec-20 (down from 114% in Mar-20); Firm HQLA comprised of eligible cash and securities totaling about $697 billion vs net cash outflows of about $634 billion; net excess eligible HQLA around $62–66 billion.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 166% (Mar-21), 160% (Dec-20), 117% (Mar-20); net excess eligible HQLA rose to ~$443 billion.
  - Eligible HQLA securities are predominantly U.S. Treasuries, U.S. GSE/agency MBS, and sovereign bonds.
- Describes drivers of changes: deposit growth—largely influenced by government actions related to COVID-19—increased bank liquidity and Firm net cash outflows; bank-level excess liquidity is excluded from Firm LCR.
- Notes that Firm LCR fluctuates with changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows due to ongoing business activity.
- Details other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities of ~$841 billion at Mar-21 (up from ~$740 billion at Dec-20), reflecting higher CIB trading assets and excess HQLA at the bank.
  - Available borrowing capacity of ~$301 billion at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window at Mar-21 (vs ~$307 billion at Dec-20); the discount window is not viewed as a primary liquidity source.
- Introduces the NSFR: final U.S. rule effective July 1, 2021 requires at least 100% NSFR on an ongoing basis, with semi-annual public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR starting in 2023; the Firm estimates it is compliant with the 100% minimum.
text:
NSFR
The net stable funding ratio (“NSFR”) is a liquidity 
requirement for large banking organizations that is intended 
to measure the adequacy of “available” and “required” 
amounts of stable funding over a one-year horizon. On 
October 20, 2020, the federal banking agencies issued a final 
NSFR rule under which large banking organizations such as 
the Firm will be required to maintain an NSFR of at least 
100% on an ongoing basis. The final NSFR rule will become 
effective on July 1, 2021, and the Firm will be required to 
publicly disclose its quarterly average NSFR semi-annually 
beginning in 2023. 
The Firm estimates that it is compliant with the 100% 
minimum NSFR  which becomes effective July 1, 2021, based 
on its current understanding of the final rule.

title: Sources of funds
heading: Sources of funds
start_phrase: Management believes that the Firm’s unsecured and secured funding capacity is sufficient to meet its on- and off-balance sheet obligations.
summary:
- Management asserts the Firm’s unsecured and secured funding capacity is sufficient for on- and off-balance sheet obligations.
- Funding is diversified: primary reliance on deposits at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; additional bank funding via short- or long-term secured borrowings, unsecured long-term debt, and intercompany borrowings (Parent Company or IHC). Non-bank subsidiaries rely mainly on long-term unsecured and short-term secured borrowings (including repos and securities lending).
- Excess funding is deployed by Treasury and CIO into the investment securities portfolio or held in cash/short-term liquid investments based on interest rate and liquidity risk.
- Deposits are a stable funding source; consumer deposits and wholesale operating deposits (tied to operating service relationships) are considered especially stable.
- Deposit trends and levels:
  - Total Firm deposits increased to $2.278T at March 31, 2021 (from $2.144T at December 31, 2020).
  - Average deposits for Q1 2021 were $2.225T vs $1.636T in Q1 2020, reflecting broad inflows across LOBs.
  - LOB period-end deposits at March 31, 2021: CCB ~$1.038T; CIB ~$726.7B; Commercial Banking ~$295.7B; Asset & Wealth Management ~$217.5B; Corporate ~$0.3B.
  - Average balances are viewed as more representative over time, though market disruptions can affect trends.
- Loans and ratios:
  - Loans totaled $1.011T at March 31, 2021.
  - Loans-to-deposits ratio declined to 44% (from 47% at December 31, 2020).
  - Deposits were 67% of total liabilities (vs 69% at December 31, 2020).
- Key drivers of deposit growth included government actions related to COVID-19, lower consumer spending, and account growth (notably in CCB).
- Additional detail on deposit and liability trends is referenced in Business Segment Results (pp. 18–34) and Consolidated Balance Sheets Analysis (pp. 12–13).
text:
Sources of funds
Management believes that the Firm’s unsecured and 
secured funding capacity is sufficient to meet its on- and 
off-balance sheet obligations.
The Firm funds its global balance sheet through diverse 
sources of funding including stable deposits, secured and 
unsecured funding in the capital markets and stockholders’ 
equity.  Deposits are the primary funding source for 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. Additionally, JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A. may also access funding through short- or long-
term secured borrowings, through the issuance of unsecured long-term debt, or from borrowings from  the 
Parent Company or the Intermediate Holding Company 
(“IHC”). The Firm’s non-bank subsidiaries are primarily 
funded from long-term unsecured borrowings and short-
term secured borrowings, primarily securities loaned or 
sold under repurchase agreements. Excess funding is 
invested by  Treasury and CIO  in the Firm’s investment 
securities portfolio or deployed in cash or other short-term 
liquid investments based on their interest rate and liquidity 
risk characteristics.

The global balance sheet is funded through diversified sources: stable deposits, secured and unsecured capital markets funding, and stockholders’ equity.

- Entity-level funding mix:
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: Primarily funded by deposits; can also access short- and long-term secured borrowings, issue unsecured long-term debt, or borrow from the Parent Company or IHC.

- Deposits:
  - Deposits are a stable funding source, with a significant share from consumer deposits and wholesale operating deposits tied to operating service relationships.

  - Short-term secured funding is primarily repos and securities lending secured by high-quality collateral (U.S. Treasuries, agency/GSE MBS).
  - Repo balances increased due to higher secured financing of AFS investment securities in Treasury and CIO, higher trading assets in CIB, and client activity.
  - Balances in repos/securities lending fluctuate with client investment/financing needs, the Firm’s liability mix management, and market/portfolio factors.
  - Short-term unsecured funding comprises other borrowed funds and commercial paper; commercial paper issuance rose to support liquidity needs.

title: Short-term funding
heading: Short-term funding
start_phrase: The Firm’s sources of short-term secured funding primarily consist of securities loaned or sold under agreements to repurchase.
summary:
- Purpose and scope: Summary of JPMorgan Chase’s non-deposit funding mix as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, plus average balances for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020.
- Short-term unsecured funding: Comprised of commercial paper and other borrowed funds; increased to $27.6B from $20.5B, driven by higher commercial paper outstanding ($15.2B vs. $12.0B) due to net issuance for short-term liquidity management.
- Short-term secured funding: Dominated by securities sold under repurchase agreements and securities lending; rose to $337.9B from $247.9B, primarily reflecting higher secured financing of available-for-sale investment securities in Treasury and CIO, higher trading assets in CIB, and client activity; balances are variable due to client financing needs, the Firm’s liability mix management, and market/portfolio factors.
- Long-term unsecured funding: Includes senior notes, subordinated debt, and structured notes (some TLAC-eligible); essentially flat at $261.9B vs. $263.0B.
- Long-term secured funding: Includes credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, and secured structured notes; declined to $21.9B from $23.6B; average FHLB advances notably lower in Q1 2021 vs. Q1 2020 (reflecting reduced reliance on this source).
- Equity: Preferred stock of $31.6B and common stockholders’ equity of $249.2B at March 31, 2021.
- Averages (Q1 2021 vs. Q1 2020) highlight mix shifts: short-term secured funding averages higher ($335.1B vs. $271.4B), commercial paper slightly lower on average ($12.9B vs. $14.0B), and FHLB advances markedly lower ($13.7B vs. $27.1B).
- Footnotes and classifications: Repo and securities lending are primarily short-term; certain items are recorded as beneficial interests of consolidated VIEs; “other borrowed funds” include nonrecourse MMLF advances; structured notes include TLAC-eligible debt; references provided to related 10-Q/10-K notes and sections for further detail.

Short-term funding 
The Firm’s sources of short-term secured funding primarily 
consist of securities loaned or sold under agreements to 
repurchase. These instruments are secured predominantly 
by high-quality securities collateral, including government-
issued debt and U.S. GSE and government agency MBS.  
Securities sold under agreements to repurchase increased at 
M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, compared with D e c e m b e r   3 1 ,  2 0 2 0, 
reflecting higher secured financing of AFS investment 
securities in Treasury and CIO, as well as higher trading 
assets in CIB, and  the impact of client activities in CIB.The balances associated with securities loaned or sold under 
agreements to repurchase fluctuate over time due to 
investment and financing activities of clients, the Firm’s 
demand for financing, the ongoing management of the mix 
of the Firm’s liabilities, including its secured and unsecured 
financing (for both the investment securities and market-
making portfolios), and other market and portfolio factors.
The Firm’s sources of short-term unsecured funding consist 
of other borrowed funds and issuance of wholesale 
commercial paper.  The increase in commercial paper at 
M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, from D e c e m b e r   3 1 ,  2 0 2 0 was due to 
higher net issuance primarily for short-term liquidity 
management.

title: Long-term funding and issuance
heading: Long-term funding and issuance
start_phrase: Long-term funding provides an additional source of stable funding and liquidity for the Firm.
summary:
- Focus: The firm’s long-term funding strategy, composition, issuance activity, and maturities/redemptions for the quarter ended March 31, 2021 (with comparisons to 2020), plus subsequent issuance and secured funding sources.
- Strategy and objectives: Long-term funding supports stable liquidity and regulatory requirements (including TLAC). The plan is driven by client activity, liquidity needs, and regulations, aiming for diversification, broad market access, and optimized costs across markets, tenors, and currencies.
- Issuance structure: The Parent Company issues the significant majority of long-term unsecured funding to support both bank and non-bank subsidiaries; it advances substantially all net proceeds to the IHC. The IHC does not issue debt to external parties. Certain Parent Company issuances are TLAC-eligible.
- Unsecured funding activity (Q1 2021 vs Q1 2020):
  - Parent Company issuance: $13.5bn (vs $9.4bn), primarily senior notes in U.S. ($9.25bn) and non-U.S. ($2.79bn) markets; structured notes $1.5bn; no subordinated debt.
  - Parent Company maturities/redemptions: $4.67bn (vs $6.99bn).
  - Subsidiaries issuance: $10.5bn structured notes (vs $9.25bn); no senior note issuance; no subordinated debt.
  - Subsidiaries maturities/redemptions: $8.58bn (vs $13.45bn); minimal senior note maturities in 2021.
- Subsequent event: After March 31, 2021, the Parent Company issued approximately $16bn of senior notes.
- Secured long-term funding sources: Consumer credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, and other secured long-term funding (including secured structured notes).
  - Issuance: $138mm in Q1 2021 (vs $16.23bn in Q1 2020, driven by $15bn FHLB advances and $1bn credit card securitization).
  - Maturities/redemptions: $1.73bn in Q1 2021 (vs $8.61bn in Q1 2020).
- Scope note: Client-driven loan securitizations in wholesale businesses are excluded as they are not a funding source for the firm.
text:
Long-term funding and issuance
Long-term funding provides an additional source of stable 
funding and liquidity for the Firm. The Firm’s long-term

liquidity considerations, and regulatory requirements,

maintaining diversification, maximizing market access and 
optimizing funding costs. The Firm evaluates various 
funding markets, tenors and currencies in creating its 
optimal long-term funding plan.
